title: What Did Ancient Humans Do in the Middle of the Night?

format.transitions: HARD CUTS ONLY — zero crossfades, dissolves or fades

narration.takes: ONE continuous take with word-level timestamps

sources: Ekirch, A. R. (2001). Sleep We Have Lost: Pre-Industrial Slumber in the British Isles. American Historical Review 106(2), 343-386.
Ekirch, A. R. (2005). At Day's Close: Night in Times Past. W. W. Norton.
Dijk, D-J. & Skeldon, A. C. (2015). Human sleep before the industrial era. Nature.
Wehr, T. A. et al. (1990s). NIMH photoperiod / biphasic sleep laboratory work.
Boyce, N. — re-examination of the segmented sleep evidence.
Yetish, G. et al. (2015). Natural sleep and its seasonal variations in three pre-industrial societies. Current Biology (Hadza, San, Tsimane).
National Museum of Denmark — Dental health in the Mesolithic period.
Trinkaus, E. & Villotte, S. (2017). External auditory exostoses and hearing loss in the Shanidar 1 Neandertal. PLOS ONE.
accuracy_notes: Segmented sleep is documented in pre-industrial Europe and early America — NOT claimed as universal.
The 'Beautyrest invented 8 hours in 1938' myth is deliberately excluded; brief.md forbids it.
Boyce's critique and the Hadza/San/Tsimane findings are included as counter-evidence on screen.
